US application in the pockets (along with convection) after conduction on the cylinders appears more favorable resulting in reasonable improvements in drying rate and energy intensity for all three basis weights. There are practical limitations related to applying US in the pockets and they need to be considered in the future. These results warrant further exploration of US and convection and potential application in the pockets. Improvements in drying rates and energy intensity as a function of moisture content and US transducer frequencies have been obtained. These correlations can be used to simulate improvements in the pockets of multi-cylinder sections. The above results were further verified by evaluating the performance of continuous (separate) application of US in conjunction with convection and compared with only convection. This is similar to what has been reported in the literature in other applications such as food drying (Rodríguez, O. et al. 2014). A general behavior of decreased drying time and improved drying rates was observed in paper and board confirming the prior reports with food materials (Figure 14 and Figure 15). Figure 14. It is clear from the US experiments that US applications are more effective at lower basis weights. US application in paper and board appears to be effective throughout the drying period. It should be noted that the above experiments were conducted using four transducers in contact with the 8x8 paper sample and the contact area coverage is approximately 20% of the total paper sample area. Given that the area coverage of the transducers on the paper samples is only ~20%, the actual improvements in drying rates and energy intensities for the whole sheet application are estimated to be 4x to 5x of the results reported. Optimal Integration of RF and US The optimal integration of RF and US in conjunction with alternating conduction and convection drying (i.e. multi-cylinder drying) was then evaluated. It is interesting that the base case multi- cylinder drying at 150 C heated platen, convection air at 100 C and 5 m/s corresponding to machine speed of 1000 FPM shows the characteristic drying rate behavior. With optimal integration of RFUS technology we were able to alter the drying rate profile and improve the overall drying performance. Periodic application of RF and US optimally integrated between conduction and convection cycles is considered a potentially viable approach to improve drying on the paper machine.
